short: Nevada has no omnibus AI act, but 2025 brought a real mental health AI restriction, an election deepfake disclosure law, and enforcement reach through existing privacy and consumer protection statutes.
title: Nevada AI Laws
subtitle: No omnibus AI act, but real narrow laws on AI in mental health and election deepfakes, plus existing privacy and consumer protection statutes that already reach AI.
body_html:
Nevada has no omnibus AI act comparable to Colorado's or Texas's, but calling the state unregulated would be wrong. In its 2025 session the Legislature passed a real restriction on AI in mental and behavioral health care, a disclosure requirement for AI-generated content in election materials, and a rule limiting AI's role in emergency decisions, while a much broader AI regulation bill died in committee. On top of that, Nevada's existing consumer protection, health data privacy, and insurance oversight laws already reach a lot of AI-driven conduct even though none of them mention AI by name.

What the legislature did

The 83rd Session (2025) saw a wave of AI-related bills, and a handful actually became law. Assembly Bill 406, sponsored by Assemblymembers Jovan Jackson and Hanadi Nadeem, restricts the use of artificial intelligence in mental and behavioral health services, barring school counselors, psychologists, social workers, and other licensed providers from using AI systems to make therapeutic or diagnostic decisions and setting civil penalties for violations. It passed both chambers with near-unanimous votes, was signed on June 5, 2025, and took effect June 6, 2025 as Chapter 283. Assembly Bill 325 requires that emergency management plans keep AI from making final decisions on disaster response, resource allocation, or utility shutdowns, and became law effective October 1, 2025. Assembly Bill 73, brought by the Secretary of State's office, requires disclosure when campaign and election communications use AI-generated or synthetic media, and takes effect January 1, 2026, making it Nevada's closest thing to a deepfake election law. Senate Bill 263 extended existing child exploitation statutes to computer-generated and AI-created content.

Not everything survived. Senate Bill 199, sponsored by Senator Dina Neal, was the session's most ambitious attempt at broad AI oversight, covering AI company registration, insurer and landlord restrictions, and a school AI working group, but it stalled in committee without a floor vote. Assembly Bill 271 would have barred AI from voting and ballot-counting systems and required disclosure of AI-generated political material, but it missed the first committee deadline and died, its disclosure piece later absorbed into AB73. Senate Bill 128, which would have barred health insurers from using AI alone to deny prior authorization requests, passed both chambers but was vetoed by the Governor on June 10, 2025. Several smaller bills on AI in tax administration, education, and patient communications also failed to advance. In the 2023 session, Nevada passed Senate Bill 370, the Nevada Consumer Health Data Privacy Law, which does not regulate AI directly but covers health information "inferred or emergent" through an algorithm or machine learning.

What already applies without a dedicated AI act

Nevada's Deceptive Trade Practices Act, NRS Chapter 598, is broad enough to cover false or misleading claims made about or by AI products, and it is the law the Attorney General's Bureau of Consumer Protection would use against an AI vendor that misrepresents what its system does. NRS Chapter 603A, the state's security and privacy of personal information law, reaches AI in two ways. The 2023 health data privacy amendments require consent before collecting data "derived through an algorithm, machine learning or any other means" when it relates to a person's health. Separately, Nevada's 2017 online privacy law lets consumers opt out of the sale of information collected about them online, regardless of whether that information was processed by AI. On the insurance side, the Nevada Division of Insurance issued a bulletin in early 2024 adopting the NAIC's model bulletin on AI use by insurers, putting carriers on notice that decisions touching consumers, including those made with AI tools, must still comply with Nevada's unfair trade practices and insurance code even without a new statute.

What the Attorney General has done

No dedicated AI enforcement action, settlement, or consumer alert from the Nevada Attorney General's office was found as of this writing. The office's general consumer protection authority under NRS 598 would apply to deceptive AI claims, but nothing AI-specific has surfaced publicly yet.

What this means

Nevada took a narrow, sector-by-sector approach in 2025 rather than a single AI law, and it worked: the mental health restriction and the election disclosure rule are real, binding obligations today, while the broadest bill failed. Anyone offering AI-driven mental health tools, running AI-assisted political ads in Nevada, or selling AI systems to insurers or emergency managers should treat these as live compliance requirements. Everyone else in Nevada is still covered by the same consumer protection and privacy statutes that predate AI, which means deceptive AI marketing or careless handling of algorithmically inferred health data can already draw legal exposure even without an omnibus AI act on the books.
